Paul of Samosata
PAWL uhv suh-MOH-suh-tuh
noun (proper name; heresiarch)
Paul, bishop of Antioch, called "of Samosata" from his birthplace on the Euphrates; a third-century teacher condemned for denying the true deity of Christ.

📖 Biblical Definition

Paul of Samosata was bishop of Antioch in the latter half of the third century and one of the early heretics whom the church condemned for denying the eternal deity of the Son. His error was a form of what is called Monarchianism or adoptionism: to guard the oneness of God, he taught that the Word and the Spirit were not distinct Persons but powers of the one God; that Jesus was a mere man, born of Mary, upon whom the divine Word or Wisdom rested as an indwelling power; and that this man, by his obedience, was exalted and adopted into a kind of divine sonship — not the eternal Son made flesh, but a man taken up. He is reported also to have lived in worldly pomp and to have suppressed hymns that praised Christ as God. The Synods of Antioch examined him and, about A.D. 268, deposed and excommunicated him; he clung to his see only under the protection of Queen Zenobia of Palmyra until Rome retook the city. His memory remained a watchword for the adoptionist heresy, and his case sharpened the church's confession of the eternal, true, and proper deity of the Son. This dictionary names his teaching as a denial of Christ that empties the gospel of its Savior.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A third-century bishop of Antioch condemned for adoptionism — the denial that Jesus is the eternal Son made flesh, teaching instead that He was a mere man upon whom the divine Word rested as a power and who was exalted to sonship. Deposed by the Synods of Antioch (c. A.D. 268).

PAUL OF SAMOSATA, proper noun. Bishop of Antioch in the latter third century, condemned as a heretic.

Taught a form of Monarchianism / adoptionism to guard the oneness of God.

Denied that the Word and Spirit are distinct Persons; made Jesus a mere man indwelt by a divine power.

Taught that this man was exalted and adopted into divine sonship, not the eternal Son incarnate.

Deposed and excommunicated by the Synods of Antioch, c. A.D. 268.

📖 Key Scripture

John 1:1 — "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God."

John 8:58 — "Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am."

Col 1:17 — "And he is before all things, and by him all things consist."

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The adoptionism of Paul of Samosata — Jesus a good man whom God exalted, not God the Son made flesh — never died; it lives in every modern theology that honors Jesus as the best of men, a divine teacher, or a Spirit-filled prophet, while denying that He is, in His own person, eternal God.

expand to see more

The corruption of Paul of Samosata is adoptionism: the denial that the Son is eternally and truly God, replacing the incarnation of the eternal Word with the exaltation of a mere man. Scripture leaves no room for it. The Word who was made flesh was, in the beginning, God (John 1:1, 14); the Son says "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58); He is before all things, and by Him all things consist (Col 1:17). A Christ who began as a man and was promoted to deity is not the Christ of the Bible and cannot save.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the historical record, but Samosata's heresy has many living heirs: liberal Christologies that make Jesus a uniquely God-conscious man, Unitarian denials of His deity, and the cults that crown Him a created exalted being. The principle to recover is the eternal, true, and proper deity of the Son — not adopted but begotten, not exalted into Godhead but eternally God, made flesh for our salvation. The church deposed Paul of Samosata because the gospel itself was at stake.
